materials.item: a table of assorted objects: keys, paper clips, coins, rubber bands, foil, plastic toys

name: Magnetic Scavenger Hunt
safety: Keep magnets away from phones and tablets, and warn kids not to swallow small magnets — ever.
setup: Lay out a table of mixed objects, half magnetic and half not. Hand out one magnet per kid or pair.
steps: Let kids freely test objects with their magnets — sort finds into magnetic and not-magnetic trays.
Ask the group to spot the pattern: what do the magnetic ones have in common?
Round two: hide ten magnetic objects around the room and hunt with magnets.
Debrief: magnets attract iron, nickel, and cobalt — not all metal.
Bonus challenge: can a magnet pull a paper clip through paper? Through a hand?
tagline: Hunt the room with a magnet and discover what metal really means.

variations.easier: Test only the objects on the table — skip the hiding round.
variations.harder: Predict first, test second: write guesses before touching the magnet.

name: Balloon Rocket Race
safety: Balloons can pop — keep them away from faces while inflating, and pick up popped pieces right away.
setup: Thread string through a straw and stretch it tight across the room, taping both ends. Build one lane per team.
steps: Tape a straw to the top of an uninflated balloon — the straw rides the string.
Inflate the balloon (do not tie it), pinch the end, and clip it to the lane's start.
Countdown and release. The escaping air drives the rocket down the line.
First rocket to the far end wins the heat. Run a bracket.
Engineering round: redesign with two balloons, angled straws, or lighter tape.
tagline: A balloon, a straw, and a string — the fastest physics demo in the room.

variations.easier: One lane, one rocket at a time — just watch it go.
variations.harder: Cargo challenge: the rocket must carry a paper-clip passenger the whole lane.

materials.item: coins or small blocks as weights

name: Paper Bridge Challenge
safety: No running with scissors if you cut paper — and keep the testing area clear so bridges do not get stepped on.
setup: Set two stacks of books about 8 inches apart as the 'river banks.' Hand out paper and a short strip of tape each.
steps: The challenge: span the gap with paper and hold as many coins as possible.
Give 15 minutes of building — folding, rolling, and corrugating are all legal.
Test one bridge at a time: lay it across the banks and stack coins in the middle.
Record each bridge's coin count on a class chart.
Winner's debrief: what shape held the most — and why?
tagline: Five sheets of paper, one gap, as many coins as it can hold.

variations.easier: Allow unlimited tape and skip the coin test — longest span wins.
variations.harder: Two sheets only, and the bridge must hold a full cup of water.

materials.item: tissue paper cut into butterfly shapes
a wool cloth or sweater for charging

name: Static Butterflies
safety: Keep balloons away from faces; rub the balloon on cloth, not on hair, to keep it simple.
setup: Cut butterfly shapes from tissue paper ahead of time — or let older kids cut their own. Lay them on a table.
steps: Rub a balloon on a wool cloth for 10 seconds to charge it with static.
Hold the charged balloon just above a tissue butterfly — it lifts and dances without touching.
Challenge: keep the butterfly floating for 10 seconds without it landing.
Test what kills the magic: does a wet butterfly still fly? A heavy one?
End with a butterfly ballet: everyone floats theirs at once to music.
tagline: Static electricity makes tissue butterflies dance.

variations.easier: One big group demo with a single balloon and butterfly.
variations.harder: Race: guide your butterfly across the table using only the balloon.

name: Water Cycle in a Bag
safety: Bags hang on the window — tape them well so nobody slips on a fallen, wet bag.
setup: Tape zip bags to a sunny window. Give each kid a marker and a small cup of water.
steps: Draw a sun and clouds on the upper part of the bag with the marker.
Pour in a quarter-cup of water and seal the bag tight.
Tape the bag to the window and predict what will happen.
Check twice a day: droplets form on the plastic (condensation) and slide down (precipitation).
After a few days, draw the cycle on the board and label each step the class observed.
tagline: The whole water cycle, sealed in a bag on the window.

variations.easier: One class bag everyone watches together.
variations.harder: Two bags — one in sun, one in shade — and compare condensation speed.

materials.item: a wide tub or bin of water
assorted test objects: apple, rock, sponge, coin, cork, toy boat

name: Sink or Float Lab
safety: Water stays in the tub — towels on the floor, no splashing contests, and dry hands before walking.
setup: Fill a wide tub halfway with water on a towel-covered table. Gather a tray of test objects.
steps: Hold up each object and vote: sink or float? Tally predictions on a chart.
Drop the object in and watch. Cheer for the right predictors.
Pull it out and dry it before the next test.
After ten objects, ask: what did the floaters have in common?
Final test: can you make a sinker float by changing its shape (foil boat challenge)?
tagline: Vote, drop, splash — the classic first experiment.

variations.easier: Test five big, obvious objects only.
variations.harder: Add a third vote option: 'sink slowly' — and time the slow sinkers.

materials.item: blank postcards or half-sheets of cardstock

name: Appreciation Postcards
safety: Keep notes kind and specific — no backhanded compliments, and nobody has to read theirs aloud.
setup: Hand out one postcard per kid. Everyone draws a name — or the teacher assigns so nobody is missed.
steps: Write one specific appreciation: something the person did, not just 'you are nice.'
Decorate the front of the card to match the message.
Drop cards in a mailbox box at the front of the room.
Deliver: read your card privately first, then the group does a thank-you round.
Pin favorites on the wall for the week.
tagline: One specific thank-you per kid, delivered like mail.

variations.easier: Sentence starters on the board: 'I noticed you...'
variations.harder: Write the card in the voice of a newspaper headline about that person.

materials.item: a long roll of butcher paper

name: Class Mural Project
safety: Smocks or old shirts for painters, and wash hands before touching anything else.
setup: Roll butcher paper across a long table or the floor. Sketch a light theme outline — a garden, a city, a galaxy.
steps: Assign sections: every kid owns one square foot of the mural.
Sketch first in pencil — no paint until the sketch is approved by a neighbor.
Paint the mural together over the session.
Add everyone's name or handprint along the border.
Hang it where the whole school can see it.
tagline: One square foot per kid, one giant story on the wall.

variations.easier: Coloring-style: the teacher draws the outlines, kids fill them in.
variations.harder: No talking during painting — the mural must come together silently.

materials.item: a list of interview questions (made together)

name: Community Helper Interviews
safety: Interviews happen with the helper visiting the group — kids do not go off alone to find people.
setup: Invite a community helper (custodian, crossing guard, nurse, librarian) or pick a staff member everyone knows. Prepare questions as a class.
steps: Brainstorm interview questions together: pick the ten best.
Assign roles: two interviewers, one note-taker, one photographer, the rest are the audience.
Welcome the guest and run the interview — 15 minutes max.
Thank the guest with a round of applause and a handmade card.
Write-up: the group turns the notes into a one-page profile for the wall.
tagline: Interview a real community helper, publish the profile.

variations.easier: Interview a staff member the kids already know well.
variations.harder: Kids run the whole interview with zero teacher help.

name: Secret Kindness Missions
safety: Missions must be kind and safe — no pranks, no touching other people's stuff without asking.
setup: Write a dozen kindness missions on slips and drop them in a jar. Each kid draws one.
steps: Examples: compliment three people, help clean without being asked, teach someone a skill you have.
Missions stay secret — nobody announces what they drew.
Give the group a set time (one session or one day) to complete their mission.
Debrief in a circle: share one kind thing you SAW, not one you did.
End by voting on the kindest moment of the day.
tagline: Secret missions, all kindness, zero pranks.

variations.easier: Everyone gets the same mission at the same time.
variations.harder: Missions for the whole week, with a Friday reveal.

materials.item: a tarp, old blanket, or large sheet of paper per team

name: All Aboard Raft
safety: Feet only on the raft — no jumping on, and keep hands to yourself while balancing.
setup: Lay out one tarp or blanket per team of 6–8 on the floor or grass.
steps: The whole team must stand on the raft for 10 seconds without anyone touching the ground.
Easy? Fold the raft in half and try again.
Keep folding — half, quarter — until it seems impossible.
Let teams strategize: carrying each other and creative balancing are allowed.
Debrief: what worked — and what did the team learn about asking for help?
tagline: The whole team on the tarp. Then fold it in half.

variations.harder: Silent round — no talking while shrinking the raft.

name: Greeting Ritual Design
safety: Greetings are always optional — a wave or a nod counts, and nobody has to touch.
setup: No materials. The group will invent its own way of saying hello.
steps: Brainstorm: how do teams greet each other — handshakes, waves, secret signals?
Each small group invents a 5-second greeting ritual with a name.
Groups perform their greeting for the class.
Vote on one to adopt as the official class greeting for the month.
Practice it at the door tomorrow morning.
tagline: Invent the class handshake — then use it every morning.

variations.easier: Pick from three teacher-suggested greetings instead of inventing.
